title: What a Plant Hanger Actually Costs. Cord, Hours, and the Price of Patience
body: A plant hanger is a small thing. Four cords, a ring, a row of knots, two hours of an evening. When people ask me to make one, they usually ask what it costs, and they expect an answer about cord. So here is the full accounting, the one I actually keep, for the piece in the photograph of my mind. The one every maker has made ten times. The cord comes first. Three millimeters, natural cotton, the workhorse of this craft. A single hanger eats about thirty meters. At street prices that lands somewhere between two and four units of money depending on where you live and whether you buy the giant spool or the small craft-store bundle. The ring is pocket change. Beads, if you use them, another small coin. Call the raw materials three units at the honest middle. The hours are the part nobody prices. Two hours for a simple hanger, but that number is a lie for a beginner and a different lie for an experienced hand. For a beginner it is four, and the four include undoing. Undoing is the real curriculum of knotwork. The square knot that pulled asymmetric, the gathering wrap that wandered, the half hitch that looked fine until it did not. You untie and retie, and the cord remembers every pass, and somewhere in the third undoing your hands learn what your eyes were too slow to see. For the experienced maker the two hours shrink, but they do not become easy. They become precise. The tension of every pass has to match its sisters across the whole piece, because tension is the actual material of this craft. Cord is just the medium that tension lives in. A hanger with uneven tension sags to one side within a month, and no amount of cord quality saves it. So the object that costs three units of materials carries, embedded in its knots, some amount of evening, some amount of undoing, and a form of patience that is difficult to buy anywhere at any price. Compare it to the factory version, which costs less than the cord and hangs perfectly forever. The comparison is not unfair; it is just measuring different things. The factory hanger holds the plant. The handmade one holds the hours, and a small record of the hands that learned on it. This is why makers keep making. Not because the economics beat the factory. They never will, and any maker who tells you otherwise is rounding something. We make because the object is a receipt. Every finished piece is proof of a capability that cannot be taken back, and capabilities, unlike objects, compound. If you are standing at the edge of this craft, or any hand craft, here is the beginner arithmetic that actually matters. Your first piece will be ugly. Price it anyway. Four hours, three units of cord, and the discovery that your hands are teachable. That is the cheapest tuition you will ever pay for a skill that stays for life. And the question I ask everyone who tells me they are not the crafting type. What did your hands learn to do that your phone cannot do for you? Because that list, in my experience, is exactly as long as you have made it so far.
